body:
from claude:

Correcting the "Possibly related" section above: my guess that this shares a mechanism with #2372 is probably wrong, and I would rather nobody spent time chasing it.

A genuine #2372 instance turned up an hour later, in a local full run on this same branch (commented there). It is one *pattern* binding the same name twice — `let y:: y = () in y` — and the two engines disagree only by an alpha-variant, `y` vs `y'`. A diff between two rendered results.

This issue is not that shape. The counterexample here has repeated *type declarations* (`type x = ()` appearing twice), not a duplicate binder in a single pattern, and the failure is an exception rather than a mismatch between two renderings. The similarity I read into it was just "the generator emitted repeated names", which is true of most terms it produces.

Also worth recording: in that local run, case 005 failed with the #2372 signature while case 007 — this issue — passed. Two distinct flakes in the same group within a day, both on a commit that touches no evaluator code.

from claude:

Second instance, and this one came with CI passing on the very same commit — which is the clearest statement yet that this is seed-dependent rather than code-dependent.

Local run on `fumola-livelit-mvp` at `f8f8a28050`, `qcheck random seed: 25926731`:

```
test `Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit`
failed on >= 1 cases:
(0, (let _ = ({ let true = y; let 2 = 98 }) in fun ? -> (()))(()))
(after 9 shrink steps)
```

CI on that same commit: green, 20m17s. So the two disagree purely by seed.

### A shape worth noting

Both counterexamples so far are full of **literal patterns in let bindings**, which is suggestive given the property is specifically about a *literal* edit:

- seed 955690280: `let _ = 0`, `let _ = B`, `let A = 1261828.579156`, `let ? = A`
- seed 25926731: `let true = y`, `let 2 = 98`, `fun ? -> (())`

`let true = y` and `let 2 = 98` are bindings whose pattern is a literal that need not match. I have not checked whether the incremental and fresh engines agree about a failed pattern match here, but that is where I would look first: the edit the property makes is to a literal, and these are the terms where a literal is load-bearing.

That is a reading of two counterexamples, not a diagnosis.

### Running count

Three failures observed across today: this property twice (seeds 955690280, 25926731) and #2372 once. Every one on a commit whose diff does not touch the evaluator, and every one alongside a green run of the identical code.

Heads-up for anyone triaging from this issue later: the "case 7" above is about to stop meaning this test.

#2482 disables this property and pins #2457 with a deterministic counterexample, and it inserts two pinned tests into the `Evaluator.Properties` list. That renumbers everything from index 6 on:

| index | on `dev` today | after #2482 |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | Evaluator and stepper are consistent | same, skipped (#2128) |
| 6 | Pattern equivalence | pin: known bug #2128 |
| 7 | **Incremental eval agrees with fresh eval after a literal edit** (this issue) | **Pattern equivalence** (#2397) |
| 8 | Preservation of types (disabled) | this property, skipped (#2457) |
| 9 | — | pin: known bug #2457 |
| 10 | — | Preservation of types (disabled) |

`dev` side read off the `tests` list; the right-hand column is from an actual run of the group on 98721df.

So post-merge, a CI failure reported as `Evaluator.Properties` case 7 is #2397 — the OOM that aborts the run — not this one. Those two are easy to conflate and the whole point of the "Not the same as #2397" section above was to keep them apart, so the index swapping between them is worth knowing about. This property will be skipped at case 8, and case 9 is the pin that reddens when #2457 is actually fixed.

Separately: this is very likely a duplicate of #2457 — same property, and #2482 cites the same failure mode. Worth closing as a dup once that lands, with the seed here (955690280) kept on #2457 as another repro.
